paragraphs: Training becomes a different computational problem when the dataset cannot fit into memory: the learner must manage both optimization and the cost of accessing data. Earlier work addressed this setting for linear support vector machines using updates to blocks of variables. This paper extends that strategy to regularized empirical risk minimization, a broader formulation that combines a data-fitting loss with a regularization term.

The framework uses strong duality and an augmented Lagrangian technique to establish global convergence for convex losses and convex regularizers. Its practical attraction is flexibility: a solver designed for data that fits in memory can be incorporated into the framework to produce a solver with convergence guarantees under limited memory.

Experiments cover classification and regression with L1 regularization. They support the convergence theory and show better performance than the compared methods adapted from online and distributed learning on datasets ten times larger than available memory. The contribution connects a general convex optimization guarantee with an approach designed around the realities of data access.
neurips-2015-a-dual-augmented-block-mini.tldr: A flexible block optimization framework extends convex learning algorithms to datasets larger than memory while retaining global convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization methods are usually described as sequences of updates. This paper studies them through a complementary picture: a point moving continuously toward an optimum according to a differential equation. It combines the continuous-time motivation behind mirror descent with an ordinary differential equation interpretation of Nesterov acceleration.

For convex functions with Lipschitz gradients, the authors propose a family of continuous-time descent dynamics with a guaranteed O(1/t²) convergence rate. The smoothness assumption controls how quickly gradients can change. Within this setting, the result gives a precise relationship between elapsed time and progress toward the optimum.

The authors then connect these continuous trajectories to implementable algorithms by discretizing the differential equation. A large family of first-order accelerated methods emerges this way, with O(1/k²) convergence in the number of iterations. The value of the connection is methodological as well as theoretical: one continuous-time description provides an intuitive route to designing and analyzing multiple accelerated algorithms, rather than treating each update rule as an isolated construction.
neurips-2015-accelerated-mirror-descent-.tldr: Continuous-time mirror descent dynamics provide a unified route to accelerated first-order algorithms with O(1/k²) convergence for the studied convex problems.

paragraphs: Accelerated proximal gradient methods are effective for convex optimization, but their usual form does not provide an established critical-point convergence guarantee for general nonconvex problems. This paper addresses objectives that can also be nonsmooth, a combination that arises in signal processing, statistics, and machine learning.

The authors introduce a monitor-corrector step and develop two versions of accelerated proximal gradient. One requires the objective to decrease monotonically. The other relaxes that requirement and uses less computation per iteration. This creates two ways to incorporate acceleration while controlling its behavior in the more general optimization setting.

The guarantee is that every accumulation point is a critical point; it does not establish that nonconvex problems reach a global optimum. When the problem is convex, the algorithms retain an O(1/k²) convergence rate. Numerical results also support a speed advantage. Together, these findings extend the reach of accelerated proximal methods while preserving a distinction between the guarantees available for convex and nonconvex objectives.
neurips-2015-accelerated-proximal-gradie.tldr: A monitor-corrector step extends accelerated proximal gradient methods to nonconvex, nonsmooth problems with critical-point guarantees and retained convex acceleration.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering often predicts missing entries in a matrix by assuming that the observed variables share a lower-dimensional structure. This paper asks how to use additional information about relationships between those variables. It represents known pairwise relationships as a graph and incorporates that graph into the matrix completion problem.

The computational contribution is an alternating minimization scheme built around conjugate gradients. Alternating minimization divides the optimization into successive subproblems, while the conjugate gradient component supports efficient solution. The authors report handling more than 55 million observations and running up to two orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art gradient-based methods used in their comparisons.

The paper also connects these methods to a broader mathematical formulation, showing that they generalize weighted nuclear norm approaches and deriving statistical consistency guarantees. Validation uses both real and synthetic data. These results make the contribution more than a speed improvement: the framework brings graph information, scalable optimization, and statistical justification into the same approach to recovering missing entries.
neurips-2015-collaborative-filtering-wit.tldr: Graph-informed matrix completion combines statistical consistency guarantees with an alternating solver reported to be up to two orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: This paper develops a convolutional neural network whose inputs are graphs, allowing a prediction pipeline to work directly with structures of arbitrary size and shape. In the molecular setting, the central question is how to turn that structured input into features useful for prediction. The proposed network makes feature construction part of the learning process.

The architecture generalizes molecular feature extraction based on circular fingerprints. This connection grounds the learned representation in an established approach to describing molecules, while allowing the features to be shaped by data. Because the pipeline can be trained end to end, representation learning and prediction become parts of one trainable system.

The authors report that the resulting features are more interpretable and provide better predictive performance across a variety of tasks. These findings support learning molecular fingerprints from data and operating directly on graph structure. The contribution is both architectural and representational: it expands the kinds of inputs convolutional networks can handle and makes molecular feature extraction adaptable to prediction.
neurips-2015-convolutional-networks-on-g.tldr: Graph convolutional networks learn molecular fingerprints end to end, with reported improvements in interpretability and predictive performance.

paragraphs: Matching items across domains is difficult when their features cannot be compared directly. Documents in different languages, for example, may describe corresponding content using different words. This paper assumes each item is represented as a multiset of features and develops a kernel method for discovering correspondences between such items.

The method first places features from different domains into a shared latent space. It then treats each item as a distribution of its features in that space. Kernel embeddings provide an efficient, nonparametric representation of those distributions, making distribution-level comparison the basis for matching. Training brings paired items' distributions closer while keeping unpaired items apart.

Experiments examine multilingual Wikipedia articles, documents paired with tags, and images paired with tags, with reported high matching performance. The approach matters because the shared representation addresses the lack of a direct cross-domain similarity measure. Representing an item through its feature distribution also preserves the paper's bag-of-features formulation while providing a common mathematical object for comparison across domains.
neurips-2015-cross-domain-matching-for-b.tldr: A shared latent space and kernel embeddings of feature distributions enable matching between bag-of-features items from different domains.

paragraphs: Marginal MAP inference seeks the most probable prediction while accounting for latent variables or missing information. It combines two operations: summing over uncertainty and maximizing over predictions. The paper addresses the difficulty of this combination, which is substantially harder than performing either pure marginalization or pure MAP inference.

The authors extend dual decomposition to a more general powered-sum inference task. Marginal MAP, marginalization, and MAP all appear as special cases, giving the framework a common language for different inference queries. Its algorithm performs block coordinate descent on a newly developed convex decomposition bound. The algorithm has guaranteed monotonic convergence and supports efficient parallel execution.

Tests on real-world problems from the UAI approximate inference challenge show faster and more reliable behavior than the previous methods considered. The guarantee concerns optimization of the decomposition bound, rather than an assertion of exact marginal MAP solutions. The contribution provides a unified optimization framework that combines a controlled convergence process with practical gains across several types of inference.
neurips-2015-decomposition-bounds-for-ma.tldr: A convex decomposition bound unifies several inference tasks and enables parallel optimization with monotonic convergence.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns class labels to individual image pixels, but training data can provide different levels of detail. Some images identify only which classes are present, while others label pixels. This paper designs a neural architecture that uses both forms of annotation by separating image classification from segmentation.

A classification network first identifies the labels associated with an image. A separate segmentation network then performs binary segmentation for each identified label, deciding which pixels belong to that class. The networks can be learned separately from image-level and pixel-level labels, respectively. Bridging layers supply class-specific activation maps that help narrow the segmentation search space.

On PASCAL VOC, the authors report strong performance relative to other semi-supervised methods despite using substantially fewer images with detailed annotations. The finding supports the architectural choice to give the two annotation types distinct roles. Image-level supervision helps establish what is present, while the segmentation component uses detailed supervision to learn where an identified class appears.
neurips-2015-decoupled-deep-neural-netwo.tldr: Separate classification and segmentation networks use mixed annotation types to deliver strong segmentation results with fewer pixel-labeled training images.

paragraphs: For binary classification with many discrete features, estimating the full joint distribution of inputs and labels can be impractical. This paper instead builds a classifier from low-order marginals: distributions involving only small groups of variables. That setting also accommodates situations where privacy concerns prevent access to complete training records.

The proposed method uses a minimum Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi correlation principle to construct a randomized classifier. For the given marginals, the authors prove an error bound no larger than twice the optimal classifier's misclassification rate. Under a separability condition, the method becomes equivalent to randomized linear regression and leads to robust feature selection based on worst-case correlation with the target.

The computational appeal is that the proposed algorithm requires a least-squares optimization problem. Its theoretical bound resembles that of the Discrete Chebyshev Classifier, while offering computational advantages. Numerical comparisons on several UCI datasets also report lower misclassification rates. The paper therefore combines a worst-case classification guarantee, a conditional connection to regression, and empirical evidence of useful performance.
neurips-2015-discrete-renyi-classifiers-.tldr: A randomized classifier built from low-order marginals offers a factor-two error bound and, under separability, a least-squares regression formulation.

paragraphs: Variational inference relies on optimization to fit an approximate probabilistic model. This paper develops a way to use second-order information in that optimization, drawing inspiration from Gaussian backpropagation. Second-order methods incorporate curvature information, giving the optimizer more information about the objective than a gradient direction alone.

The authors generalize gradient computation in stochastic backpropagation through a lower-complexity reparameterization trick. Their approach supports Hessian-based or Hessian-free optimization, and they argue that it can also support quasi-Newton methods. They additionally derive variance bounds for estimators of otherwise intractable expectations when the functions involved are Lipschitz continuous.

Bayesian logistic regression and variational autoencoders illustrate the approach. Experiments on several real-world datasets show substantially improved convergence rates compared with the stochastic gradient methods considered. The paper presents the method as practical, scalable, and model free. Its main contribution is to make curvature-aware optimization accessible within stochastic variational inference, alongside theoretical analysis of estimator variability for a specified function family.
neurips-2015-fast-second-order-stochasti.tldr: Generalized stochastic backpropagation enables second-order variational inference optimization, with reported convergence improvements over compared stochastic gradient methods.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are useful in supervised and unsupervised learning, but their computational demands can prevent applications to large datasets. This paper introduces the Gaussian Process Random Field, an approximation intended to make large-scale Gaussian process modeling more practical while retaining connections between local models.

The construction couples local Gaussian processes through pairwise potentials. These terms connect pairs of local models within the overall approximation. The resulting likelihood approximates the full Gaussian process marginal likelihood and is designed to be tractable and parallelizable. This matters because that likelihood supports more than prediction: it also enables latent variable modeling and the selection of model hyperparameters.

The authors demonstrate the method on synthetic spatial data and a real application involving seismic event locations. These examples provide evidence that the approximation can support useful modeling in spatial settings. The central contribution is a computationally manageable likelihood built from connected local components, extending the practical reach of Gaussian process tools without requiring evaluation of the full model's marginal likelihood.
neurips-2015-gaussian-process-random-fie.tldr: Gaussian Process Random Fields couple local Gaussian processes to provide a tractable, parallelizable likelihood approximation for large-scale modeling.

paragraphs: This paper studies directed acyclic graphical models for count variables. Each node follows a Poisson distribution whose rate depends on its parents' values. The authors investigate both whether the directed model can be uniquely identified from observational data and how to learn it efficiently at large scale.

They prove identifiability for the Poisson DAG models and give a polynomial-time learning algorithm under suitable regularity conditions. The key signal is overdispersion: variables that are Poisson after conditioning can display greater dispersion than marginally Poisson variables when those dependencies are not accounted for. The algorithm uses this distinction to help recover the directed structure.

For faster computation, the approach combines overdispersion scoring with methods for learning sparse, undirected Poisson graphical models. The paper provides theoretical guarantees and simulation results on both small and large DAGs. Its significance is the connection between a specific distributional property and structure learning: within the Poisson model setting, variation in counts supplies information that can make observational identification and efficient learning possible.
neurips-2015-learning-large-scale-poisso.tldr: Overdispersion provides a signal for identifying Poisson DAGs from observational data and learning them in polynomial time under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: When the question concerns one variable's direct causes and effects, recovering the causal structure of an entire system can require unnecessary work. This paper focuses on that narrower task. It seeks the causal relationships involving a chosen target, such as a class label, without making complete global structure discovery the objective.

The proposed Causal Markov Blanket algorithm builds on Markov blanket discovery. It conducts discovery across multiple variables but concentrates on determining which relationships connect directly to the target. This local focus is the source of its intended computational advantage: the algorithm organizes its search around the information needed for the particular causal question.

Under standard assumptions, the authors provide theoretical and experimental support for identification accuracy comparable to global methods, together with substantially improved efficiency. The reported speed improvements often exceed one order of magnitude. These results support local causal discovery when the desired output is target-specific, with the accuracy claim tied to the assumptions under which the method is analyzed.
neurips-2015-local-causal-discovery-of-d.tldr: Target-focused causal discovery achieves accuracy comparable to global methods under standard assumptions, with reported efficiency gains often exceeding tenfold.

paragraphs: Some selection problems require choosing several different kinds of items while keeping the resulting groups disjoint. A k-submodular function models this situation by taking k disjoint subsets as its input, extending the single-subset formulation of ordinary submodularity. The paper studies maximizing monotone functions of this kind under restrictions on set sizes.

The authors develop constant-factor approximation algorithms for several size-constrained settings. Such guarantees establish that the returned solution achieves a fixed fraction of the optimum, without requiring exact optimization. The algorithms run in time that is almost linear in the size of the domain, making the computational cost grow relatively gently as the pool of possible items expands.

The formulation naturally covers influence maximization with multiple topics and sensor placement with multiple sensor types. Experiments report better solution quality than the baseline algorithms considered. The contribution combines three useful properties for these structured selection problems: support for multiple disjoint groups, explicit approximation guarantees, and running times suited to larger domains.
neurips-2015-monotone-k-submodular-funct.tldr: Nearly linear-time algorithms provide constant-factor guarantees for monotone k-submodular maximization under several size constraints.

paragraphs: Learning a revenue-maximizing auction from data requires balancing flexibility with learnability. A simple auction family may miss profitable mechanisms, while a more expressive family can be harder to learn reliably. This paper introduces t-level auctions to provide a controlled range between simple auction formats and optimal auctions.

The analysis separates two sources of error. Representation error measures how much revenue is lost by restricting attention to the chosen auction family. For every product distribution over bidders' valuations, the authors show that an auction with small t can obtain expected revenue close to optimal. Learning error concerns estimating a good auction from samples; modest pseudo-dimension controls this error when t is polynomial.

Together, these results imply that, in arbitrary single-parameter settings within the stated framework, a polynomial number of samples suffices to learn a mechanism with expected revenue arbitrarily close to optimal. The contribution explains why a carefully chosen intermediate auction family can be expressive enough to approximate optimal revenue while remaining statistically learnable.
neurips-2015-on-the-pseudo-dimension-of-.tldr: T-level auctions balance expressivity and statistical complexity, enabling near-optimal expected revenue learning with polynomially many samples in the studied settings.

paragraphs: Deep learning optimization must make useful updates from estimated gradients while navigating complicated objectives. This paper concentrates on how to use those gradients more effectively. It explicitly leaves the challenge of nonconvexity unresolved and instead studies how an optimizer can better account for the geometry of the objective.

The proposed approach combines preconditioning with a non-Euclidean gradient method. Preconditioning adjusts the optimization problem's effective scaling, while the non-Euclidean component changes the geometry used to determine updates. The authors contrast this combination with earlier preconditioned methods operating in Euclidean space and provide evidence that it captures objective geometry more accurately.

The paper formalizes these arguments theoretically and derives new optimization algorithms from them. Applications to restricted Boltzmann machines, feedforward neural networks, and convolutional neural networks produce promising results in computational time and solution quality. The findings support geometry-aware use of gradient estimates across several model families, while preserving the paper's narrower claim about optimization behavior rather than resolving nonconvex learning in general.
neurips-2015-preconditioned-spectral-des.tldr: Combining preconditioning with non-Euclidean gradient updates shows promise for improving deep learning optimization time and solution quality.

paragraphs: Distinguishing neural cell types helps researchers understand how a circuit processes information. In the retina, existing identification techniques can be accurate but labor intensive. This paper develops automated classifiers for retinal ganglion cells using only voltage recordings from a large-scale array, making the recorded electrical patterns the basis for functional identification.

The first classifiers operate on individual cells. Their features describe voltage waveforms across space and time, along with patterns in the intervals between spikes. These classifiers distinguish major ganglion cell classes in the primate retina well, but they do not achieve comparable accuracy for identifying ON versus OFF polarity.

The authors address that specific weakness by adding information about relationships within cell populations. Cross-correlations indicate functional coupling between cells, and a matrix completion algorithm uses those indicators to infer polarity. The results suggest that accurate, fully automated classification can emerge by combining individual electrical signatures with population-level information, rather than expecting one cell's recorded features to resolve every aspect of its identity.
neurips-2015-recognizing-retinal-ganglio.tldr: Electrical signatures identify major retinal ganglion cell classes, while population correlations help recover ON/OFF polarity through matrix completion.

paragraphs: Explicit feature maps can make kernel methods easier to scale, but accurately approximating polynomial kernels has required many features, especially for higher-degree polynomials. This paper asks whether a common preprocessing choice can help: when every input has unit Euclidean norm, all the data lies on the unit sphere.

The authors show that a proposed affirmative route using Random Fourier Features is impossible in this setting. They then introduce Spherical Random Fourier features, an alternative approximation approach designed for data on the sphere. The construction uses the normalization assumption to obtain compact approximations to polynomial kernels.

Compared with prior work, the resulting features are reported to be more compact, less rank deficient, and more accurate at approximating the kernel, with particularly strong benefits for higher-order polynomials. Predictions also have lower variance and typically better classification accuracy. The contribution shows how a known property of the input domain can shape a more effective approximation, while keeping the classification improvement appropriately qualified as typical.
neurips-2015-spherical-random-features-f.tldr: Spherical random features exploit unit-normalized inputs to approximate polynomial kernels more compactly and accurately, typically improving classification.

paragraphs: Perceptual decisions depend on noisy sensory samples, so the reliability of those samples affects how informative they are. The paper examines whether the brain takes that reliability into account when it changes unpredictably. Its approach analyzes drift diffusion models, which are frequently used to explain perceptual decision-making findings.

The authors first show that even the basic drift diffusion model implicitly depends on estimates of stimulus reliability. This makes reliability part of the model's operation even when it is not treated as an explicit additional mechanism. They then compare model variants with neurophysiological findings and conclude that only variants allowing stimulus-specific reliabilities are consistent with those findings.

The analysis suggests that the brain estimates reliability within at most a few hundred milliseconds. This timing is an inference from the analysis, rather than an unqualified assertion that every perceptual setting has the same timescale. The contribution clarifies what familiar decision models already assume and connects their treatment of noise to evidence about neural processing.
neurips-2015-the-brain-uses-reliability-.tldr: Drift diffusion model analysis suggests that perceptual decisions use stimulus-specific reliability estimates formed within a few hundred milliseconds.

paragraphs: A conventional multivariate normal distribution has an ellipsoidal shape because it measures distance using Euclidean geometry. This paper changes that underlying geometry. It introduces a smoothly varying Riemannian metric that favors regions with high local data density, allowing the distribution to follow data assumed to lie near a potentially low-dimensional manifold.

The resulting locally adaptive normal distribution, or LAND, still has a mean and covariance as its parameters, although its metric is nonparametric. The authors also characterize it as a maximum entropy distribution under the given metric. This combination preserves a compact parameterization for the distribution while allowing the surrounding geometry to adapt to the data.

To fit LAND, the paper develops maximum likelihood estimation using gradient descent and Monte Carlo integration. It also extends the construction to mixtures and supplies an expectation-maximization algorithm. Demonstrations on synthetic data and human sleep EEG measurements show its ability to fit nontrivial distributions, supporting adaptive geometry as a way to extend normal-distribution modeling.
neurips-2016-a-locally-adaptive-normal-d.tldr: LAND generalizes the normal distribution by adapting its distance geometry to local data density and manifold structure.

paragraphs: Hybrid recommenders combine rating information with item content, but handcrafted features and bag-of-words representations can inadequately capture that content. This paper develops a collaborative recurrent autoencoder that models content as ordered sequences while also learning from collaborative filtering information. Its training connects recommendation with reconstructing missing content.

The authors first formulate a denoising recurrent autoencoder as a hierarchical Bayesian model, then extend it to the collaborative filtering setting. The construction includes a new denoising scheme and a learnable pooling scheme. It also adapts recurrent modeling from independently distributed inputs to inputs connected through collaborative filtering, making the content model part of the recommendation system.

Experiments on CiteULike and Netflix report significant improvements over the compared state of the art in both rating-based recommendation and content-based sequence generation. These findings support the proposed synergy: learning to fill gaps in ordered content and learning collaborative preferences can help each other. The contribution is a joint model in which content reconstruction and recommendation are coupled learning tasks.
neurips-2016-collaborative-recurrent-aut.tldr: A collaborative recurrent autoencoder jointly learns ordered content reconstruction and recommendations, improving both tasks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Generative models can describe a joint distribution over variables, but many tasks require a distribution of outputs conditioned on a particular input. This paper introduces conditional generative moment-matching networks to learn that input-dependent distribution. It builds on the use of kernel mean embeddings and maximum mean discrepancy in deep generative modeling.

The proposed training criterion is conditional maximum mean discrepancy. It extends distribution matching to the conditional setting, so the network learns how the output distribution relates to the supplied input variables. Training uses stochastic gradient descent, with gradients computed through backpropagation, connecting the conditional criterion to standard neural network optimization.

The authors evaluate the method on predictive modeling, contextual generation, and Bayesian dark knowledge. In the last application, a relatively small student network learns knowledge from a Bayesian model. Reported performance is competitive across these tasks. The results support the same conditional distribution-learning framework for several purposes, including prediction, generation informed by context, and transferring Bayesian model knowledge into a smaller network.
neurips-2016-conditional-generative-mome.tldr: Conditional moment matching trains generative networks for input-dependent distributions, with competitive results in prediction, contextual generation, and Bayesian distillation.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced categorical responses depend both on what contributors know and on how they respond to incentives. Existing modeling approaches often emphasize one side: either honest contributors with differing error rates or strategic contributors seeking rewards. This paper develops a Bayesian model that includes differences in information quality alongside incentive-sensitive behavior.

That joint treatment connects two decisions that are often studied separately. Elicitation concerns how to obtain responses, while aggregation concerns how to combine the responses into a useful result. Because the model includes both contributor knowledge and strategic choices, it allows those decisions to be examined within the same probabilistic framework.

The authors use analytical and experimental work to investigate optimal aggregation and the design of multiple-choice interfaces. The contribution is a model that generalizes both earlier categories and supports reasoning about collection and combination together. Its significance is that interface design and aggregation can be evaluated with a shared account of the people producing the data, rather than relying on separate behavioral assumptions.
neurips-2016-eliciting-categorical-data-.tldr: A Bayesian crowdsourcing model combines unequal information quality with strategic behavior to study response collection and aggregation jointly.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet Allocation is a useful model for topics and other hidden groups, but choosing the number of groups can be difficult. Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes address an unknown topic count through a nonparametric extension. This paper seeks a simpler alternative that makes the distribution over the number of topics explicit.

The authors introduce two extensions of LDA that directly represent uncertainty about topic count. That choice addresses a difficulty they identify in HDP: its implicit distribution over topics makes prior knowledge difficult to incorporate. They also develop online Bayesian moment matching to learn both model parameters and the number of topics as data arrives in a stream.

Across several corpora, the approach achieves higher log-likelihood than the compared batch and online HDP methods with fixed hyperparameters. This is a comparison under that stated configuration. The contribution combines an explicit treatment of topic-count uncertainty with streaming inference, offering a more direct modeling formulation and reported gains in how well the learned models explain the data.
neurips-2016-online-bayesian-moment-matc.tldr: Two LDA extensions explicitly model topic-count uncertainty and use online Bayesian moment matching to learn from streaming data.

paragraphs: Interpreting inputs with multiple objects requires deciding which features belong together. Tagger makes that grouping process an explicit part of neural inference. It learns grouping without requiring a specific segmentation target, either through unsupervised learning or alongside a supervised task, and its framework does not require image inputs.

A differentiable mechanism iteratively groups representations of different objects. The system amortizes the joint inference of group assignments and representations, learning to carry out that iterative process efficiently. The authors report very fast convergence. This design makes grouping a trainable component of perception rather than a separate fixed preprocessing stage.

Evaluation uses heavily cluttered multi-digit images requiring texture segmentation. Despite being fully connected, the system improves classification over convolutional networks by using its grouping mechanism. It also substantially improves on a baseline Ladder network's semi-supervised result on the authors' dataset. These findings provide evidence that explicit grouping can improve sample efficiency, with the empirical support coming from the evaluated multi-object image setting.
neurips-2016-tagger-deep-unsupervised-pe.tldr: Tagger learns iterative object grouping and improves classification and semi-supervised results on cluttered multi-digit images.
